 About 

# About Monowar Hossain

 My name is Monowar Hossain . I am a WordPress plugin developer from Dhaka, Bangladesh, known online as devmonowar — I maintain six free plugins on WordPress.org, published since 2021, with the source on GitHub. 

## Who I am

 I build things for WordPress, and almost all of it is free and open source — anyone can download it, read the code, and change it. Twelve public repositories carry the work, and every plugin goes through the WordPress.org review before release. 
 Right now I maintain a set of plugins published on WordPress.org, and I run a shared demo library that shows what every ready-made demo looks like before anyone imports it. 

## How I started

 I finished a Diploma in Engineering at Magura Polytechnic Institute in 2016. I did not begin with WordPress. I started with plain HTML and CSS, then moved to PHP because I wanted to understand what was actually happening behind the pages I was putting together. 
 WordPress kept me for one simple reason: when something did not work the way I wanted, I could open the code and fix it. That is exactly how my first plugin began. I needed a slider that did not slow a site down, I could not find one I was happy with, so I wrote my own. Later I cleaned it up and published it on WordPress.org so other people could use it too. 

## How I work

 Every plugin I have released follows the same three rules, and they came from problems I hit myself. 
 
 Load only what the page needs. A plugin should not add CSS and JavaScript to pages that do not use its feature. This is the single most common reason a WordPress site gets slow, and it is avoidable. 
 Do one job properly. I would rather ship a plugin that does testimonials well than an addon pack with dozens of widgets where you use three and pay for the weight of the rest. 
 Be honest about limits. If a plugin cannot be certain about something, it should say so instead of guessing. That idea shaped Janitorix Media Audit completely — it refuses to recommend deleting an image unless it can show the evidence behind that verdict. 

## What I build and why

 None of these started as a product idea. Each one started as something that annoyed me on a real site. 
 
 General Slider — I needed a slider that loads fast and still works for someone using a keyboard or a screen reader. Most sliders are heavy and skip the accessibility part entirely. 
 Advanced Testimonial — a client wanted the same customer reviews in several places on their site, each in a different layout. Copying the text meant several places to update every time a review changed. 
 Free Widgets For Elementor — Elementor's free version is missing a few widgets nearly every site needs. The usual fix is a giant addon pack. I built [a focused alternative](/blog/free-widgets-for-elementor-guide/) instead. 
 Janitorix Media Audit — media libraries fill up with images no page uses any more, and the existing cleanup tools mostly guess. Leaving an unused image costs a few kilobytes; deleting one that is still referenced breaks the site. Those two mistakes are not equal, so the plugin does not treat them as equal. The method it uses is written out in full: [how to find unused images in WordPress](/blog/how-to-find-unused-images-in-wordpress/). 
 CrawlWatch – AI Bot Insights — AI assistants had been reading my site for months and I had no way of knowing it. Analytics does not count a crawler, and the server log is not something most site owners will ever open. So the plugin logs those visits, shows which pages were taken, and lets you allow or block each bot without writing a line of robots.txt by hand. 
 ScheduleLens – Cron Viewer & Manager — WordPress runs its scheduled jobs invisibly, so a missed schedule always looks like some other bug. I wanted one screen that lists every job in plain words and lets me run or pause it there — and a health check that admits when the quiet site itself is the problem. 

## Open source

 I keep my work free because that is how I learned. When I was starting out I read other people's plugin code to figure out how WordPress really worked. That code was free for me, so mine is free too. 
 Free does not mean unfinished. Every plugin goes through [the WordPress.org review](/blog/wordpress-plugin-review-what-they-flagged/) before release, ships with documentation and a changelog, and I answer the support topics on the forum myself. If something is broken, I would much rather hear about it and fix it. 

## What I am learning now

 Two things have most of my attention. The first is performance — how to keep a plugin small enough that adding it to a site is not a trade-off. I wrote up [what actually makes a WordPress slider slow](/blog/why-wordpress-sliders-are-slow/) and how to measure it yourself. The second is accessibility, which I did not take seriously enough early on: making sure what I build works with a keyboard and a screen reader, not only with a mouse. 
 Writing the guides on this site is part of how I work on both. Explaining something to another developer is the fastest way to find out whether I actually understand it — and it is usually while writing the steps down that I notice the one I had been getting away with.

# Plugins

 Everything here is free, GPL licensed, and open source. There is no Pro version, no licence key, and no upgrade prompt in any of them. The plugins on WordPress.org were reviewed by the WordPress.org team before release. 

## General Slider

 A slider that does not slow your site down. 
 A slider sounds like a simple feature, but it is one of the most common places a WordPress site picks up weight it does not need — jQuery dependencies, render-blocking CSS, and JavaScript that runs on every page even when there is no slider on it. 
 General Slider is built on [Splide](https://splidejs.com/), a lightweight slider engine with no dependencies. There is no jQuery on the front end, and the CSS and JavaScript are only added to pages that actually contain a slider. 
 
### What it does

 Build a slider once, then drop it anywhere with a block, a shortcode, or an Elementor widget 
 Works without a page builder — the block and shortcode work with any theme 
 Pull slides automatically from your latest posts, pages, or WooCommerce products 
 Design presets and navigation skins you can mix freely, plus per-slide background video and an accent colour 
 Keyboard and screen-reader accessible by default 
 Images lazy-load, and a slider only starts once it is scrolled into view 

 [Download on WordPress.org](https://wordpress.org/plugins/general-slider/)
 [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/devmonowar/general-slider)
 [See the demos](https://devmonowar.github.io/wp-plugin-demo-library/general-slider/)
 [Full guide](/blog/general-slider-fast-accessible-wordpress-slider/)
 [General Slider - fast WordPress slider without jQuery](/general-slider/)

## Advanced Testimonial

 Customer reviews, added once and shown anywhere. 
 Most WordPress testimonial solutions force a trade-off. Basic plugins give you one static layout and no way to collect new reviews. All-in-one page-builder addon packs bury a testimonial widget inside dozens of others you will never use, adding weight to every page on the site. 
 Advanced Testimonial is built only for testimonials. Reviews get their own post type with Groups, and each review carries its own fields — rating, company, verified badge, video. It ships with Schema.org review markup, so Google can show star ratings next to your search result. 
 
### What it does

 Several display layouts — grid, list, card, carousel, marquee, masonry and spotlight 
 A set of card styles you can mix, with a different style per block if you want 
 A front-end form so visitors can submit their own review, with spam protection built in 
 Submissions arrive as pending, so nothing goes live before you approve it 
 Group testimonials so different pages can show different sets 
 Video testimonials from YouTube, Vimeo or a self-hosted file, opened in a lightbox 
 Your testimonials are never deleted on uninstall unless you explicitly opt in 

 [Download on WordPress.org](https://wordpress.org/plugins/advanced-testimonial/)
 [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/devmonowar/advanced-testimonial)
 [See the demos](https://devmonowar.github.io/wp-plugin-demo-library/advanced-testimonial/)
 [Full guide](/blog/advanced-testimonial-wordpress-testimonials-guide/)
 [Advanced Testimonial - WordPress testimonials plugin](/advanced-testimonial/)

## Free Widgets For Elementor

 The widgets Elementor's free core is missing. 
 If you have built more than a couple of sites with the free version of Elementor, you have hit this wall: you need a pricing table, or a flip box, or a simple countdown timer, and the free core does not have them. The usual fix is installing a giant addon pack that ships dozens of widgets when you need three. 
 This plugin adds only what the free core is actually missing — nothing you already have, nothing you will not use. Each widget's CSS and JavaScript load only on the pages where that widget is used. 
 
### What is inside

 Pricing Table — header, price, feature list, button, optional featured highlight 
 Flip Box — a 3D hover or click flip to a back face with a call to action 
 Team — photo, role, bio and social links for team member cards 
 Call To Action — title, text, button and background in a styled box 
 Countdown Timer — counts down to a date and time, with an optional expired message 
 Post Grid — a responsive grid of posts with image, title, meta, excerpt and read-more 
 Logo Carousel — a responsive logo carousel with arrows, dots and autoplay 
 Table of Contents — an auto-generated page outline with smooth scroll and scrollspy 
 
 Elementor Pro is not required, and there is no locked feature anywhere in it. A built-in demo library lets you import ready-made sections in one click. 
 
 [Download on WordPress.org](https://wordpress.org/plugins/free-widgets-for-elementor/)
 [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/devmonowar/free-widgets-for-elementor)
 [Full guide](/blog/free-widgets-for-elementor-guide/)
 [Free Widgets For Elementor - extra Elementor widgets](/free-widgets-for-elementor/)

## Janitorix Media Audit

 Proves an image is unused before it suggests deleting it. 
 Every WordPress media library fills up with images nobody uses any more — old banners, replaced logos, test uploads. Most cleanup plugins scan the uploads folder, flag whatever looks unused, and hand you a delete button. 
 The trouble is that the cost of being wrong is not symmetric. Leaving an unused image costs a few kilobytes. Deleting one that is still referenced somewhere — a Customizer background, an ACF field, a page-builder section — breaks your site, and you might not notice for weeks. 
 
### How it is different

 Janitorix Media Audit never blends "is this used?" into a single guess. Every image gets two separate judgements: 
 
 Confidence — how sure the plugin is that the image is genuinely unused, based on scanners covering post content, Gutenberg blocks and synced patterns, full-site-editing templates, the Customizer, theme options, widgets, menus, Elementor, ACF, WooCommerce, and the theme's own PHP, CSS and JavaScript files. 
 Risk — how much damage deleting it would cause if the plugin is wrong . 
 
 A site logo nobody explicitly references and a stray test upload can score identically on confidence, but they need opposite treatment. That is why risk is scored on its own. 
 
### What it refuses to do

 Will not recommend deleting anything if scan coverage was too low — it asks for a rescan instead 
 Will not offer Trash for anything at medium risk or above, however confident the scan is 
 Will never touch a site's logo, icon or header — those are refused outright, not just scored low 
 Will not touch an image uploaded in the last 24 hours 
 Never deletes in one step — Trash first, always 
 
 It is free and open source, and the whole review that got it into the directory is written up in [what the WordPress.org plugin review flagged](/blog/wordpress-plugin-review-what-they-flagged/). 
 
 [Download on WordPress.org](https://wordpress.org/plugins/janitorix-media-audit/)
 [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/devmonowar/janitorix-media-audit)
 [How to find unused images](/blog/how-to-find-unused-images-in-wordpress/)
 [Janitorix Media Audit - find unused images in WordPress](/janitorix-media-audit/)

## CrawlWatch – AI Bot Insights

 Shows you the traffic your analytics never mentions. 
 GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and Google-Extended read your site every day, and none of it shows up in a normal analytics dashboard. You cannot tell which pages they took, whether anyone arrived from an AI assistant afterwards, or whether your site is worth reading in the first place. 
 CrawlWatch logs those visits and puts them somewhere you can see them. It recognises more than forty AI crawlers, and every visit is stored in one table on your own server. There is no API key, no account, and no external service. 
 
### What it does

 Shows which AI bots visited and exactly which URLs they read 
 Tracks referrals — visitors arriving from ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini or Claude 
 Generates llms.txt and ai.txt in one click, with a full-content version for deeper context 
 Allows or blocks each AI bot in robots.txt from a preview screen, with no code 
 Scores how ready your site is for AI readers, from 0 to 100, and ranks the quickest fixes 
 Blocking an AI training bot does not touch Google search — regular Googlebot is never managed here 

### What it does not do

 Sends nothing off your server — every row lives in one local table 
 Never stores a raw IP address; they are hashed, and truncated before hashing 
 Adds no CSS or JavaScript to the front end, and a normal human visit costs zero extra queries 
 Keeps logs for 30 days by default, and deletes older rows on a daily schedule 
 
 One thing worth knowing before you install it: tracking runs in PHP, so a full-page cache that serves a page without running PHP will hide those visits. The plugin detects the common caching plugins and says so on its own screens rather than quietly showing you an empty chart. 
 
 [Download on WordPress.org](https://wordpress.org/plugins/crawlwatch-ai-bot-insights/)
 [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/devmonowar/crawlwatch-ai-bot-insights)
 [Full guide](/blog/ai-bot-traffic-wordpress/)
 [CrawlWatch - AI bot traffic insights for WordPress](/crawlwatch-ai-bot-insights/)

## ScheduleLens – Cron Viewer & Manager

 Every cron job in plain words. 
 WordPress runs dozens of scheduled jobs in the background, and there is no screen that lists them. When one silently stops, the symptom shows up somewhere else — a post that never publishes, a check that never runs. 
 ScheduleLens is that screen. Every event with its repeat interval, next run time, and which plugin added it — overdue jobs badged red, core jobs gray. Run a job now, pause it without deleting it, add a custom job without code, and check wp-cron health with fix steps on the same screen. 
 
### What it does

 Lists all cron events with repeat, next run, and source plugin 
 Run now, Pause / Resume, Delete custom jobs — core jobs protected 
 Adds custom jobs without code (existing hook only, no PHP execution) 
 Health tab: enabled, reachable, late count, total — Green / Yellow / Red with fix steps 
 Keeps a log of the last 100 runs with duration, auto-pruned after a few days 
 Admin pages only — no CSS or JavaScript on the front end, no tracking 

 [Download on WordPress.org](https://wordpress.org/plugins/schedulelens-cron-viewer/)
 [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/devmonowar/schedulelens-cron-viewer)
 [ScheduleLens - WordPress cron job viewer](/schedulelens-cron-viewer/)

 General Slider 

# General Slider — a WordPress slider without jQuery

 By Monowar Hossain 
 Rated 5.0 out of 5 from [2 reviews](https://wordpress.org/support/plugin/general-slider/reviews/) on WordPress.org 
 12 September 2026 

 Summary. General Slider is a free WordPress slider plugin with no jQuery on the front end. It is built on the lightweight Splide engine. It is keyboard and screen-reader accessible out of the box, and its files load only on pages that actually show a slider. No Pro version, no locked features. 

## Why no jQuery matters

 Most slider plugins pull in jQuery whether your theme needs it or not. That is a whole library downloaded, parsed and run on every page — including the ones with no slider on them. On a site that already dropped jQuery, a slider plugin quietly puts it back. 
 General Slider never asks for it. The front end runs on [Splide](https://splidejs.com/), a slider engine with no dependencies of its own, so a page without a slider gets nothing at all: no script, no stylesheet. I measured where slider weight actually comes from in [why WordPress sliders are slow](/blog/why-wordpress-sliders-are-slow/) — the short version is that the images are rarely the problem. 

 A hero slider on the front end — heading, text, button, arrows and dots, no page builder involved. 

## What it does

 Build a slider once, then place it with a block, a shortcode, or an Elementor widget 
 Five design presets — hero, split, minimal, testimonial, fullscreen — mixed freely with navigation and frame skins 
 Per-slide background video, text entrance animations and an accent colour, all without code 
 Dynamic sliders that build themselves from your latest posts, pages or WooCommerce products 
 Separate settings for tablet and phone, so a slider that looks right on desktop stays right on a phone 
 Images lazy-load and a slider only starts once it is scrolled into view 
 One-click demo import — each demo installs as a draft you can publish when it looks right 

 Every preset and skin, side by side in the demo library — each one imports in a single click. 

## Sliders that update themselves

 If your slider just shows the latest posts, rebuilding it by hand every week gets old fast. Switch the slides source to dynamic and the slider reads your posts, pages or products itself — new content shows up on its own, and nothing is frozen into the slider when the source changes. 

## Free means free here

 There is no Pro version of this plugin and there never will be. Every preset, every skin and the demo library ship in the free download from WordPress.org, and the settings screen contains no upgrade prompt. If you have used a slider where the design you actually want sits behind a paywall, that frustration is exactly what this plugin does not do. 

## FAQ

 Is there a Pro version? 
 No. Everything is in the free plugin, and there is no licence key or upgrade prompt anywhere in it. 

 Does it work with block themes? 
 Yes. The block works in the editor and in full-site-editing templates, and the shortcode works anywhere else, with any theme. 

 Can a slide have a video background? 
 Yes. Each slide can carry its own background video, set from the slider settings without code. 

 Will it slow down pages that have no slider? 
 No. The CSS and JavaScript are only added to pages that actually contain a slider. 

 Can I try it before installing? 
 Yes. The [demo library](https://devmonowar.github.io/wp-plugin-demo-library/general-slider/) shows every preset and skin, and each demo imports into your own site in one click. 

## Download it or read the walkthrough

 If you want the full walkthrough — install, first slider, presets, and the three mistakes almost everyone makes — that is the [step-by-step guide](/blog/general-slider-fast-accessible-wordpress-slider/). If you just want the plugin, it is one search away in your dashboard.

 [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/devmonowar/general-slider)

 Janitorix Media Audit 

# Janitorix Media Audit — an unused image cleaner that proves it first

 By Monowar Hossain 
 Rated 5.0 out of 5 from [2 reviews](https://wordpress.org/support/plugin/janitorix-media-audit/reviews/) on WordPress.org 
 12 September 2026 

 Summary. Janitorix Media Audit finds the images in your WordPress media library that nothing uses — then shows its evidence before it suggests deleting anything. Every file gets two separate scores, one for confidence and one for risk, and the plugin only ever moves files to Trash. Free, no Pro version. 

## Deleting is cheap until it is wrong

 Every media library fills up the same way: old banners, replaced logos, test uploads, the three spare photos from a post that used one. Leaving them costs a few kilobytes each. Deleting one that is still referenced — a Customizer background, an ACF field, a page-builder section — breaks a page you might not open for weeks. 
 Most cleanup tools treat those two mistakes as equal. They scan, they flag, they hand you a delete button. This plugin starts from the opposite end: the cost of being wrong is the whole design. That is why "is this used?" is never one answer here. It is two. 

## Two scores, not one guess

 Each image is checked by scanners covering post content, Gutenberg blocks and synced patterns, full-site-editing templates, the Customizer, theme options, widgets, menus, Elementor, ACF, WooCommerce, and the theme's own PHP, CSS and JavaScript files. The result comes back as two judgements: 
 
 Confidence — how sure the plugin is that the image is genuinely unused. 
 Risk — how much damage deleting it would cause if the plugin is wrong . 
 
 A stray test upload and an unreferenced site logo can score identically on confidence and need opposite treatment. That is why risk is scored on its own, and why anything at medium risk or above is never offered for Trash at all. 

 What the scanners are up against: a reference can live in six different places, and they do not all store the same thing. 

## What it refuses to do

 Will not recommend deleting anything if scan coverage was too low — it asks for a rescan instead 
 Will never touch a site logo, icon or header — refused outright, not just scored low 
 Will not touch anything uploaded in the last 24 hours — it may not have been placed yet 
 Never deletes in one step — Trash first, always, so anything can be restored 

## For the terminal-inclined

 The whole thing also runs from WP-CLI: scan the library, ask why one image got the verdict it did, preview exactly what would be deleted without deleting anything, and calibrate the engines against known answers. The read-only preview is the same evidence the admin screens show, in CSV form. 

## FAQ

 Does it delete images permanently? 
 No. It only ever moves files to Trash, so anything can be restored. There is no one-click permanent delete. 

 What if the plugin is wrong about an image? 
 That is what the risk score is for. Anything at medium risk or above is never offered for Trash, however confident the scan is. 

 Will it touch my logo or header image? 
 No. The site logo, icon and header are refused outright, as is anything uploaded in the last 24 hours. 

 Can I run a scan from WP-CLI? 
 Yes. Scan, explain, preview deletions and calibrate — all from the command line. 

 Is there a Pro version? 
 No. Confidence and risk scoring, Trash-only cleanup and WP-CLI — everything is in the free plugin, reviewed by the WordPress.org team before release. 

## Understand first, or install first

 If you want to understand the problem first — where a reference can hide and how to check one image by hand — that is the [full guide](/blog/how-to-find-unused-images-in-wordpress/). If you want the tool, it is one search away in your dashboard. 
 
 [Download on WordPress.org](https://wordpress.org/plugins/janitorix-media-audit/)
 [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/devmonowar/janitorix-media-audit)

 Advanced Testimonial 

# Advanced Testimonial — a testimonial plugin that collects its own reviews

 By Monowar Hossain 
 Rated 5.0 out of 5 from [1 review](https://wordpress.org/support/plugin/advanced-testimonial/reviews/) on WordPress.org 
 12 September 2026 

 Summary. Advanced Testimonial is a free WordPress plugin built only for customer reviews. It stores them properly, shows them in seven layouts with mixable card styles, collects new ones through a front-end form, and adds the Schema.org markup Google needs for star ratings. No page-builder addon pack, no Pro version. 

## The usual trade-off, skipped

 The hard part of testimonials is rarely showing them. It is getting them — asking customers, collecting their words, approving each one — without pasting every quote in by hand or installing an addon pack of dozens of widgets for a single job. 
 This plugin is one thing instead: testimonials, done completely. Reviews get their own post type with Groups, and each review carries its own fields — rating, company, verified badge, video — and visitors can submit their own through a form. Nothing else rides along. 

 A review grid on the front end — photos, half-star ratings, companies, each card styled on its own. 

## Reviews that arrive on their own

 The part most testimonial plugins skip is collection. Here a [at_form] shortcode drops a submission form anywhere, with a honeypot and rate limiting built in so it does not become a spam magnet. Submissions arrive as pending and stay there until approved — nothing goes live by accident, and the export only ever covers published reviews. 

## Shown anywhere, styled per spot

 Seven layouts — grid, list, card, carousel, marquee, masonry and spotlight — through a block, a shortcode or an Elementor widget. Card styles mix freely, including a different style per block, and Groups mean the homepage and the pricing page never have to show the same set. Ratings support half stars, and video reviews from YouTube, Vimeo or a self-hosted file open in a lightbox. 

 Three cards, three styles — picked per block, not per site. 

## Stars Google can read

 Every review carries Schema.org markup, so eligible pages can show star ratings right in the search results. That is the quiet half of social proof: the reviews persuade on your page, and the stars persuade before anyone clicks. 

## FAQ

 How do new reviews get collected? 
 Through a front-end submission form with spam protection built in. Submissions arrive as pending, so nothing goes live before you approve it. 

 Can review stars show in Google search results? 
 Yes. The plugin ships Schema.org review markup, so Google can show star ratings next to your pages in search results. 

 Can different pages show different reviews? 
 Yes. Reviews are organised into Groups, so the homepage, the pricing page and the contact page can each show their own set. 

 How are testimonials displayed? 
 Seven layouts — grid, list, card, carousel, marquee, masonry and spotlight — through a block, a shortcode or an Elementor widget, with mixable card styles. 

 Is there a Pro version? 
 No. Layouts, card styles, the review form and the schema markup — everything is in the free plugin, reviewed by the WordPress.org team before release. 

## Walkthrough or demos first

 If you want the full walkthrough — setup, displaying, collecting, and the mistakes to avoid — that is the [step-by-step guide](/blog/advanced-testimonial-wordpress-testimonials-guide/). If you want to see the layouts first, the demos are one click away. 
 
 [Download on WordPress.org](https://wordpress.org/plugins/advanced-testimonial/)
 [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/devmonowar/advanced-testimonial)
 [Browse the demos](https://devmonowar.github.io/wp-plugin-demo-library/advanced-testimonial/)

 Free Widgets For Elementor 

# Free Widgets For Elementor — the missing widgets, nothing else

 By Monowar Hossain 
 Rated 5.0 out of 5 from [2 reviews](https://wordpress.org/support/plugin/free-widgets-for-elementor/reviews/) on WordPress.org 
 12 September 2026 

 Summary. Free Widgets For Elementor adds the widgets the free core leaves out — pricing table, flip box, team, call to action, countdown timer, post grid, logo carousel and table of contents. Each one loads its files only where it is used, any of them can be switched off, and there is no Pro version. 

## The wall free Elementor hits

 Build enough sites with free Elementor and the moment comes: you need a pricing table, or a flip box, or a plain countdown timer, and the free core simply does not have them. The standard fix is a giant addon pack — dozens of widgets installed for the three you actually wanted, every one of them loading on pages you will never put them on. 
 This plugin is the opposite bet: only what the free core is missing, nothing it already has, nothing you will not use. The free version of Elementor is enough. Pro is not required for a single thing in it. 

 The widgets sit in their own Elementor panel category — no hunting through someone else's list. 

## What is inside

 Pricing Table — header, price, feature list, button, with an optional featured highlight 
 Flip Box — a 3D flip to a back face with a call to action, on hover or click 
 Team — photo, role, bio and social links for member cards 
 Call To Action — title, text, button and background in one styled box 
 Countdown Timer — counts down to a date and time, with a message for when it expires 
 Post Grid — image, title, meta, excerpt and read-more in a responsive grid 
 Logo Carousel — arrows, dots and autoplay, responsive out of the box 
 Table of Contents — an auto-generated outline with smooth scroll and scrollspy 
 
 One thing is missing on purpose: there is no testimonial widget here. Testimonials need a post type, groups and a submission form, which is a whole plugin — my [Advanced Testimonial](/advanced-testimonial/) — not a widget. 

 A pricing table on the front end — the plan most free-Elementor sites hit the wall on first. 

## Only where it is used

 The reason a small list stays small in weight too: each widget's CSS and JavaScript load only on pages where that widget sits. And if you know you will never use one, its toggle removes it completely — a disabled widget is never even registered with Elementor, let alone loaded. 

## FAQ

 Why these widgets and not more? 
 Each one fills a gap in Elementor's free core. Nothing here duplicates a widget Elementor already gives away, which is why the list stays short on purpose. 

 Why is there no testimonial widget? 
 Testimonials need a post type, groups and a submission form — that is a whole plugin, not a widget. It already exists separately as Advanced Testimonial. 

 Do widgets I don't use still load their files? 
 No. Each widget's CSS and JavaScript load only on pages where that widget is actually used, and any widget can be switched off entirely. 

 Can I switch off widgets I don't need? 
 Yes. Every widget has its own enable toggle, and a disabled widget is never even registered with Elementor. 

 Is there a Pro version? 
 No. The plugin is free with no upsells, reviewed by the WordPress.org team before release. 

## Per-widget tour or straight to install

 If you want the per-widget tour — what each one does and how the demo import works — that is the [step-by-step guide](/blog/free-widgets-for-elementor-guide/). If you just want the widgets, they are one search away in your dashboard. 
 
 [Download on WordPress.org](https://wordpress.org/plugins/free-widgets-for-elementor/)
 [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/devmonowar/free-widgets-for-elementor)

## CrawlWatch AI Bot Insights

 CrawlWatch – AI Bot Insights 

# CrawlWatch — see which AI bots read your site

 By Monowar Hossain 
 Rated 5.0 out of 5 from [2 reviews](https://wordpress.org/support/plugin/crawlwatch-ai-bot-insights/reviews/) on WordPress.org 
 12 September 2026 

 Summary. CrawlWatch is a free WordPress plugin that logs AI-crawler visits where you can see them: which bots came, which URLs they took, and whether anyone arrived from an AI assistant afterwards. It also scores how ready your site is for AI readers, generates llms.txt , and lets you allow or block each bot — all without anything leaving your server. 

## The traffic your analytics never mentions

 GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and Google-Extended read sites every day, and none of it appears in a normal analytics dashboard. You cannot tell which pages they took, whether your content is worth reading to them in the first place, or whether a single visitor ever arrived from an AI assistant afterwards. 
 CrawlWatch puts that traffic on a screen in your own dashboard. It recognises more than forty AI crawlers, stores every visit in one table on your server, and asks for nothing in return — no API key, no account, no external service. 

 The overview: hits, bots, referrals and a readiness score — with the quickest fixes ranked underneath. 

## A score with a to-do list attached

 The readiness score runs from 0 to 100, but a number on its own never fixed anything. Underneath it sits a breakdown of what was measured — llms.txt catalogue, excerpts as AI descriptions, schema, image alt text, robots.txt, active tracking — and a short list of quick wins ordered by impact, each linking to the exact screen that resolves it. The score is the headline; the list is the point. 

## Two files, no code

 On the Files screen, llms.txt generates in one click — a catalogue version plus a full-content one — and each AI bot gets its own allow-or-block checkbox for robots.txt , with a preview before anything is saved. Blocked bots are told Disallow; the plugin only appends, so the WordPress core rules are never overwritten. And blocking a training bot touches search traffic not at all, because regular Googlebot is never managed here. 

 llms.txt on the left, per-bot robots.txt rules on the right — previewed before anything is saved. 

## One honest limitation

 Tracking runs in PHP, so a full-page cache that serves a page without running PHP will hide those visits from the log. The plugin detects the common caching plugins and says so on its own screens instead of quietly showing an empty chart. I would rather read that warning than wonder why a busy site shows no bots at all. 

## FAQ

 Which AI bots does it recognise? 
 More than forty, including GPTBot, ClaudeBot, PerplexityBot and Google-Extended. A crawler the list does not know is one the plugin cannot report, so the signature list is the first place to look when traffic goes missing. 

 Will blocking a bot hurt my Google rankings? 
 No. The screen only manages AI training and search bots. Regular Googlebot is never touched here, so search traffic is unaffected. 

 Does any data leave my server? 
 No. There is no API key and no external service. Every visit is stored in one table on your own server, IPs are hashed and truncated, and logs older than 30 days are deleted on a schedule. 

 Will it slow down my site? 
 No. It adds no CSS or JavaScript to the front end, and a normal human visit costs zero extra queries. 

 Is there a Pro version? 
 No. Bot logging, referrals, the readiness score, llms.txt and robots.txt — everything is in the free plugin, reviewed by the WordPress.org team before release. 

## Install it and give it a few days

 Install it from your dashboard like any other plugin, open the CrawlWatch menu, and give it a few days — bot traffic arrives on its own schedule, not yours. The readiness score tells you what to fix first. 
 
 [Download on WordPress.org](https://wordpress.org/plugins/crawlwatch-ai-bot-insights/)
 [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/devmonowar/crawlwatch-ai-bot-insights)

## ScheduleLens Cron Viewer

(https://devmonowar.github.io/schedulelens-cron-viewer/)

[Home](/) 
 [Plugins](/plugins/) 
 ScheduleLens – Cron Viewer & Manager 

# ScheduleLens — every cron job in plain words

 By Monowar Hossain 
 Rated 5.0 out of 5 from [1 review](https://wordpress.org/support/plugin/schedulelens-cron-viewer/reviews/) on WordPress.org 
 18 September 2026 

 Summary. ScheduleLens is a free WordPress plugin that shows every scheduled job on one screen — what runs, when it runs next, and which plugin put it there. You can run a job now, pause it without deleting it, add a custom job without code, and check whether wp-cron itself is healthy. Admin-only, no frontend load, no tracking. 

## The jobs WordPress runs when nobody is watching

 WordPress runs dozens of scheduled jobs in the background — publishing scheduled posts, checking for updates, and whatever each installed plugin queued up. When one of them silently stops, the symptom is always somewhere else: a post that never publishes, a check that never runs. And there is no screen in WordPress that lists them. 
 ScheduleLens is that screen. Every event with its repeat interval, next run time, and source — which plugin added it — in plain words, with overdue jobs carrying a red badge and core jobs a gray one so the two are never confused. 

 Every event — repeat, next run, source plugin — with overdue jobs badged red. 

## Run, pause, delete — without code

 Find the event and click Run now to fire it manually, with the run logged along with its duration. Pause keeps a job as a backup so it stops running without being deleted, and Delete removes custom jobs — core jobs are protected and the plugin blocks their deletion with a warning. A custom job can be added without writing PHP, but only by triggering a hook that already exists; executing arbitrary code was left out on purpose. Custom intervals start at a minimum of sixty seconds. 

## A health check with fix steps

 The Health tab answers the one question that matters when schedules misbehave: is wp-cron itself working? Enabled, reachable, late count and total, shown as Green, Yellow or Red — each with the fix steps next to it, such as pointing a real server cron at wp-cron.php . The last hundred runs sit in a log with durations and prune themselves after a few days, so the evidence is there when something goes wrong at three in the morning. 

 Green, Yellow or Red — and what to do about it, on the same screen. 

## One honest limitation

 WordPress cron only fires when somebody visits the site, so on a very quiet site schedules will always run late no matter what screen you watch them on. The plugin says exactly that on its own Health tab instead of pretending the schedule is fine. If your site is that quiet, the fix is a real server cron — the screen tells you so. 

## FAQ

 Why do scheduled posts miss schedule? 
 Low traffic, caching, or DISABLE_WP_CRON can stop schedules from firing. The Health tab shows whether wp-cron is enabled and reachable, with Green, Yellow or Red plus fix steps — for example setting up a real server cron that hits wp-cron.php. 

 How do I run a cron job manually? 
 Find the event under Tools, Cron Manager and click Run now. The run is logged in the Log tab with its duration. 

 Can I pause a cron job without deleting it? 
 Yes. Click Pause and the job is kept as a backup — it will not run until you resume it. Core jobs cannot be deleted; the plugin blocks that with a warning. 

 Will it slow down my site? 
 No. It runs on admin pages only and adds no CSS or JavaScript to the front end. 

 Does it send data outside my server? 
 No. Everything stays in wp_options with autoload off, and nothing personal is stored. The only request it ever makes is a loopback check to your own wp-cron.php for the Health tab. 

## Install it and open Tools, Cron Manager

 Install it from your dashboard like any other plugin, open the Cron Manager under Tools, and look at what your site has been doing behind your back. If a post ever misses schedule again, the Health tab is the first place to look. 
 
 [Download on WordPress.org](https://wordpress.org/plugins/schedulelens-cron-viewer/)
 [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/devmonowar/schedulelens-cron-viewer)

## Privacy Policy

 Privacy Policy 

# Privacy Policy

 Last updated 20 September 2026 

## This website collects nothing

 devmonowar.github.io is hand-written static HTML. There is no analytics, no JavaScript, no cookies, no contact form, and no account system — so there is nothing here that records your visit. The site is hosted on GitHub Pages; like any web host, GitHub may keep server logs. Their policy governs that, not this page. 

## The WordPress plugins, on your own site

 My plugins run on sites you control, and what they record stays there: 
 
 [General Slider](/general-slider/), [Advanced Testimonial](/advanced-testimonial/), [Free Widgets For Elementor](/free-widgets-for-elementor/), [Janitorix Media Audit](/janitorix-media-audit/) — no visitor data leaves your site. Janitorix scans your own media library and stores its verdicts in your own database. 
 [CrawlWatch - AI Bot Insights](/crawlwatch-ai-bot-insights/) — logs visits from AI crawlers (time, bot name, visited URL, referrer, truncated user-agent). IP addresses are anonymised before hashing (IPv4 last octet and IPv6 /64 removed) and never stored raw. Logs are kept 7–180 days at your choice (30 by default) and auto-deleted; everything is removed on uninstall if enabled in Settings. No visitor data leaves your site. 
 [ScheduleLens - Cron Viewer & Manager](/schedulelens-cron-viewer/) — stores its paused-jobs list, the last 100 run-log rows, custom intervals and three settings in your database. The only network call is a loopback check to your own site for the health tab. All data is deleted on uninstall if enabled in Settings. 

## Contact

 Questions about any of this: [devmonowar@gmail.com](mailto:devmonowar@gmail.com) or the [contact page](/contact/).

 Advanced Testimonial guide 

# How to add customer testimonials in WordPress: a complete guide to Advanced Testimonial

 By Monowar Hossain 
 11 August 2026 

 Summary. Social proof sells, but most WordPress testimonial plugins are either too basic — one boring layout — or bloated page-builder addons you do not need. I built Advanced Testimonial to be the focused middle ground: a set of display layouts and card styles, a front-end submission form, and Schema.org markup for star ratings in Google, all in one lightweight plugin. 

## On this page

 [One layout or fifty widgets you never use](#problem) 
 [A plugin built only for testimonials](#solution) 
 [What you need to install it](#requirements) 
 [Installing Advanced Testimonial](#install) 
 [Displaying testimonials](#display) 
 [Collecting testimonials from visitors](#collect) 
 [Choosing a layout and card style](#styling) 
 [Testimonial setup mistakes to avoid](#mistakes) 
 [FAQ](#faq) 
 [Conclusion](#conclusion) 

## One layout or fifty widgets you never use

 Testimonials are one of the highest-converting elements you can put on a page, but most WordPress solutions force a trade-off. 
 Basic plugins give you one static layout with no way to collect new reviews. All-in-one page-builder addon packs give you a testimonial widget buried inside dozens of others you will never touch, adding weight to every page on your site. 

## A plugin built only for testimonials

 Advanced Testimonial is a plugin built only for testimonials. Reviews get a proper post type with Groups, and each review carries its own fields — rating, company, verified badge, video. 
 Seven display layouts and nine card styles can be mixed freely, and the plugin ships with built-in Schema.org review markup , so Google can show star ratings as a rich snippet next to your search result. 

## What you need to install it

 WordPress 6.5 or later 
 PHP 7.4 or later 
 No page builder required. The shortcode and block editor work out of the box, and an Elementor widget is added automatically if Elementor is active. 

## Installing Advanced Testimonial

 In your WordPress dashboard, go to Plugins → Add New and search for Advanced Testimonial . 
 Click Install Now , then Activate . 
 A new Testimonials menu appears in your dashboard sidebar. 
 Add your first testimonial, or open Testimonials → Settings → Tools and use the one-click starter demo to see it working immediately. 

 Search for Advanced Testimonial under Plugins → Add New, then install and activate it. 

 The one-click demo library, if you would rather start from a ready-made set than an empty screen. 

## Displaying testimonials

 Use the shortcode anywhere: 
 [advanced_testimonial layout="grid" columns="3" group="clients" limit="9" order="desc"] 
 Or add the Advanced Testimonial block in the editor — it has the same controls with a live preview. 
 The seven available layouts are grid, list, card, carousel, marquee, masonry and spotlight. Nine card styles — classic, modern, minimal, bubble, bold, glass, gradient, outline and retro — are picked with the style attribute, and you can use a different style per block if you like. 

 The grid layout, with star ratings and verified badges on each card. 

 Every card style side by side. Mix a different one per block if you want. 

## Collecting testimonials from visitors

 Add this to any page and visitors can submit their own testimonial directly from your site: 
 [at_form title="Leave a review" group="clients"] 
 Submissions arrive as Pending , so you review them before they go live. Spam protection is built in — nonce, honeypot and rate limiting — and the defaults are safe. 

 The front-end form visitors use to leave a review. 

 Submissions land as Pending in the admin, so nothing goes live before you approve it. 

## Choosing a layout and card style

 Seven layouts and nine card styles sounds like a lot of choice, so here is how I think about it. Pick the layout for the page, and the style for the brand. 
 
 Grid for a dedicated reviews page, carousel for a homepage strip, marquee for a logo-wall effect that never stops, masonry for reviews of very different lengths. 
 Card styles (classic, modern, minimal, bubble, bold, glass, gradient, outline, retro) change the look without touching the layout — and each block or shortcode can use its own, so the homepage and the pricing page do not have to match. 
 Verified badges and photos do more for trust than any layout. A real name, a company, a face — that is what visitors read first. The layout is just the frame around it. 

## Testimonial setup mistakes to avoid

 Forgetting to group testimonials. If you plan to show different sets on different pages — per service or per product — set up Groups under Testimonials → Groups before you start adding reviews. Reorganising later is more work than doing it first. 
 Not checking the submission form settings. The defaults are safe, but if unexpected spam gets through, look at Settings → Submission Form . 
 Assuming Elementor is required. It is not. The shortcode and the block work on any theme. 

## FAQ

 Do I need Elementor to use this plugin? 
 No. The shortcode and Gutenberg block work with any theme. If Elementor is active, a widget appears automatically. 

 Can testimonials include video? 
 Yes. Paste a YouTube, Vimeo, or self-hosted MP4 URL on any testimonial and it opens in a lightbox on click. 

 Will it slow down my site? 
 No. CSS and JavaScript load only on pages that actually display testimonials, and there is no jQuery. 

 Will my testimonials be deleted if I uninstall the plugin? 
 No, not by default. You have to explicitly opt in under Settings → Advanced first. 

## Conclusion

 If you need real, manageable testimonials rather than a giant addon pack, Advanced Testimonial gives you the layouts, the styles, and a form to collect new reviews — without adding weight to pages that do not need it. 
 
 [Download on WordPress.org](https://wordpress.org/plugins/advanced-testimonial/)
 [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/devmonowar/advanced-testimonial)
 [Browse the demos](https://devmonowar.github.io/wp-plugin-demo-library/advanced-testimonial/)

## https://devmonowar.github.io/blog/ai-bot-traffic-wordpress/

(https://devmonowar.github.io/blog/ai-bot-traffic-wordpress/)

 AI bot traffic in WordPress 

# AI bot traffic in WordPress — see it, measure it, decide what to do

 By Monowar Hossain 
 16 September 2026 

 Summary. I opened my server logs one morning expecting the usual Googlebot entries and found strangers instead — GPTBot, CCBot, names I had never invited. WordPress had shown me none of it. Not a counter, not a notice, nothing. This post is what I wish I had found that morning: how to see AI bot traffic on a WordPress site, what each kind of visit actually means, and how I learned to decide per bot instead of copying somebody's blocklist. 

## On this page

 [Two kinds of AI visitors, and why they matter differently](#two-kinds) 
 [Seeing the crawlers in your logs](#see) 
 [Reading one log line](#read-line) 
 [Should you block them?](#block) 
 [robots.txt, honestly](#robots) 
 [What llms.txt is actually for](#llms) 
 [The visitors the assistants send you](#referrals) 
 [If you want a plugin to watch this](#plugin) 
 [Common mistakes](#mistakes) 
 [FAQ](#faq) 
 [Conclusion](#conclusion) 

## Two kinds of AI visitors, and why they matter differently

 Here is the confusion I see everywhere, and I had it too: people say "AI bot traffic" like it is one thing. It is two, and they want opposite things from you. 
 First come the crawlers . They fetch your pages to learn from them. GPTBot gathers training data for OpenAI. CCBot feeds Common Crawl, the nonprofit dataset half the industry trains on. Then there is ClaudeBot and anthropic-ai for Anthropic, Bytespider for ByteDance, PerplexityBot fetching pages so it can cite them in answers. None of them click anything. None of them buy anything. They take your words and leave. 
 Then there are the referrals , and these walk in the other direction. Someone asks an AI assistant a question, the assistant links to your page, and a living human being lands on your site. In analytics they look like ordinary referrals from chatgpt.com or perplexity.ai . They read. They click. Some of them convert. This is the traffic you actually want — which is why the block-or-allow question is trickier than the angry threads make it sound. 

## Seeing the crawlers in your logs

 WordPress keeps no record of who reads your site. None. No visitor log, no bot list, nothing you can open in the admin. The record lives one floor below WordPress, in the server's access log . Every hosting panel has one — look under Statistics or Metrics — and the file is usually called access.log . 
 I want to be honest about this part: the first time you open that file, it is ugly. Thousands of lines, IPs, timestamps, noise. Do not read it. Search it. Open find-in-page and type the names. The regulars: 
 
 GPTBot / OAI-SearchBot / ChatGPT-User — OpenAI, but three different jobs: GPTBot gathers training data, OAI-SearchBot decides what ChatGPT Search can cite (blocking it hides you from answers without affecting training), and ChatGPT-User fetches pages when a user explicitly asks (it generally ignores robots.txt) 
 CCBot — Common Crawl, the nonprofit dataset behind many models 
 anthropic-ai / ClaudeBot / Claude-SearchBot — Anthropic: the first two feed training, Claude-SearchBot feeds Claude search answers 
 PerplexityBot / Perplexity-User — Perplexity: the bot surfaces pages in search results (it does not train models), the user agent fetches on request 
 Bytespider — ByteDance 
 Google-Extended / Applebot-Extended — Google's and Apple's opt-out training crawlers, separate from their search crawlers 
 Meta-ExternalAgent — Meta 
 
 If your site has been up for a year, every one of these has visited. 

 Crawler What it actually governs If you block it 

 GPTBot OpenAI model training Content stays out of training data 
 OAI-SearchBot ChatGPT Search citability — not training Site disappears from ChatGPT answers 
 ChatGPT-User User-triggered fetches Usually nothing — it ignores robots.txt anyway 
 ClaudeBot Anthropic model training Content stays out of training data 
 Claude-SearchBot Claude search answers — not training Site disappears from Claude search 
 PerplexityBot Perplexity search results — not training Site disappears from Perplexity answers 
 Google-Extended Gemini and Vertex training only — never AI Overviews No effect on search or AI Overviews 
 Googlebot Search, including AI Overviews Search traffic drops — almost never what you want 

 That was the part that surprised me — not that they came, but how long they had been coming while I looked at nothing but the WordPress dashboard. The question was never whether. It was whether anyone was watching. Every name above documents itself — [OpenAI's crawler overview](https://platform.openai.com/docs/bots), [Anthropic's crawling article](https://support.anthropic.com/en/articles/8896518-does-anthropic-crawl-data-from-the-web), [Perplexity's bot guide](https://docs.perplexity.ai/guides/perplexitybot), [Google's crawler list](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/crawling-indexing/overview-google-crawlers) — so when a new name appears in your logs, its own docs are the first place to check what it actually governs. 

## Reading one log line

 A log line looks scary exactly once. Then somebody shows you where to look, and you cannot unsee it. Here is a typical one: 
 203.0.113.40 - - [12/Sep/2026:10:14:02 +0000] "GET /pricing/ HTTP/1.1" 200 48210
"-" "Mozilla/5.0 ... compatible; GPTBot/1.2; +https://openai.com/gptbot" 
 Read it left to right. An IP address. The date. The page it asked for — /pricing/ , in this case, which already tells you something, because bots that only read your homepage behave differently from bots reading your pricing page. Then 200 , meaning your server handed the page over without complaint. The bytes it carried home. And at the very end, the user-agent introducing itself as GPTBot , with a link to [OpenAI's own page about it](https://openai.com/gptbot). 
 One line is trivia. A thousand lines is a story: which bot keeps coming back, which pages it likes, whether it visits at 3am like a polite guest or hammers fifty pages a minute. And here is the catch I keep coming back to — the bots that never introduce themselves never appear in this story at all. Logs show you the honest visitors. They say nothing about the quiet ones. 

 The same log data, readable: which bots came, what they took, and what to fix first — without opening access.log ever again. 

## Should you block them?

 Most guides go quiet right here and hand you a snippet to paste. I think that is backwards. The snippet takes ten seconds; the decision deserves ten minutes. So here is how I actually think about it, both sides, no cheerleading. 
 
 The case for blocking. Your content becomes training data for products that compete with you for the same readers. Crawlers cost bandwidth — on a small VPS, an aggressive crawl is a bill and a slowdown. And there is a principle in it: your work, your permission. 
 The case against. Blocking does not remove anything already trained on; that data is baked in. Assistants that cannot read your site cite your competitors instead, and the referral visitors in the previous section go to them. For most small sites, obscurity is a bigger threat than being quoted. 
 
 My own answer, for what it is worth: I block the bandwidth hogs and the crawlers that give me nothing back, and I welcome the ones that cite pages and send actual humans. PerplexityBot can stay; it links to things. A nameless scraper pulling a thousand pages at midnight cannot. And I revisit the list about once a year, because the cast keeps changing and a decision from 2024 is not a decision, it is a habit. 

## robots.txt, honestly

 So much for the thinking. The mechanism is robots.txt — and before you trust it, you should know exactly what it is. A text file. A request. That is all. Here is what asking the major AI crawlers to stay out looks like: 
 User-agent: GPTBot
User-agent: CCBot
User-agent: ClaudeBot
User-agent: anthropic-ai
User-agent: PerplexityBot
User-agent: Bytespider
Disallow: / 
 The polite ones obey. GPTBot, CCBot, Google-Extended, most crawlers with real names on them — they check robots.txt before fetching, because ignoring it publicly would be embarrassing for a company that size. But understand what you just did: you put up a sign. There is no lock behind it and no one enforcing it. A crawler that hides its name never reads your sign, and a few named ones have been caught fetching pages they were told not to. Keep the sign up — it is correct and necessary — and then check the logs to see who listened. The log check is the part everyone forgets. 
 One thing people always ask me at this point, usually worried: will this hurt my Google rankings? No. Googlebot crawls for search under its own name, and Google-Extended — the training opt-out — is a separate user-agent entirely. Refuse one, welcome the other. Your search traffic will not move. I have done exactly this and watched Search Console stay flat. 

## What llms.txt is actually for

 If robots.txt is the keep-out sign, llms.txt is the note you leave for the guests you invited in. It is a young convention, not a standard anyone enforces: a Markdown file at /llms.txt that describes your site the way language models digest best. What the site is. What each section covers. Which pages actually matter. 
 People misunderstand the purpose, so let me say it plainly: this is not about feeding the models. They already have your pages — that battle is over. It is about accuracy . A model working from your own summary quotes you correctly. A model reconstructing you from scraped fragments invents things, confidently, in your name. I have seen my own plugin described wrong by an assistant, and it is a strange feeling. 
 The file costs an hour to write well. Whether every assistant reads it is still unsettled — conventions take years, and some may never bother. But there is no downside to having one, and the upside is being cited correctly instead of creatively. 

 Both files in one place: the generated llms.txt on the left, a per-bot allow-or-block checkbox for robots.txt on the right. 

## The visitors the assistants send you

 Now the second kind of visitor, because I suspect this number will surprise you the way it surprised me. Open your analytics, find referrals, and pull out chatgpt.com , perplexity.ai , copilot.microsoft.com and their friends. Whatever number comes out — that is your AI referral traffic . Real humans, arriving because a machine recommended you. There is something funny about that, and something worth money. 
 Two things follow from knowing the number. First, it becomes the scoreboard for everything above: if it climbs after you publish an llms.txt and keep your content quotable, the welcoming strategy is paying off. Second, these visitors arrive strange — they land mid-question, half-answered, impatient. The pages they land on should answer fast and link onward. Watch the landing pages, not just the totals. Totals flatter; landing pages teach. 

## If you want a plugin to watch this

 I will say what I always say about this category: nobody opens access logs every morning. Not you, not me, nobody with a site to run. So eventually a tool watches them for you. When you go looking for one, ignore the screenshots and ask these instead: 
 
 Does it show you which bot, which page, and how often — or just a total count? A total tells you nothing to act on. 
 Does it separate crawlers from AI referrals? A tool that mixes the two will have you blocking the visitors you wanted. 
 Does it manage robots.txt rules per bot , instead of one all-or-nothing switch? Your decision for PerplexityBot and your decision for Bytespider are not the same decision. 
 Does it write the llms.txt for you? The file is small but fiddly; generating it from your actual content beats a blank template. 
 Does everything happen on your own

 Free Widgets For Elementor guide 

# How to install Free Widgets For Elementor: the widgets Elementor's free core does not include

 By Monowar Hossain 
 11 August 2026 

 Summary. Elementor's free version is good, but it is missing a few widgets almost every site ends up needing — a pricing table, a flip box, a countdown timer, a team section. I built Free Widgets For Elementor to fill exactly those gaps, with no bloat and no upsells. Here is how to install it and what each widget does. 

## On this page

 [Elementor free is missing the widgets you need](#problem) 
 [Eight widgets, nothing you already have](#solution) 
 [What you need to install it](#requirements) 
 [Installing Free Widgets For Elementor](#install) 
 [What is inside](#widgets) 
 [Using the demo library](#demos) 
 [Why it stays fast](#performance) 
 [Widget mistakes that cost you speed](#mistakes) 
 [FAQ](#faq) 
 [Conclusion](#conclusion) 

## Elementor free is missing the widgets you need

 If you have built more than a couple of sites with the free version of Elementor, you have hit this wall. You need a pricing table, or a flip box, or a simple countdown timer, and the free core just does not have them. 
 The usual fix is installing a giant all-in-one addon pack that ships dozens of widgets when you need three — slowing the site down with unused CSS and JavaScript on every page. 

## Eight widgets, nothing you already have

 I built Free Widgets For Elementor as a focused, lightweight plugin that adds only the widgets Elementor's free core is actually missing. Nothing you already have, nothing you will not use. 
 It is fully free and GPL licensed, with no Pro version, no licence key, and no upgrade nags in the editor. Each widget's CSS and JavaScript load only on the pages where that widget is actually used, so it does not add weight to pages that do not need it. 

## What you need to install it

 WordPress 6.0 or later 
 PHP 7.4 or later 
 [Elementor](https://wordpress.org/plugins/elementor/) — the free version. Elementor Pro is not required. 

## Installing Free Widgets For Elementor

 Make sure the free Elementor plugin is installed and activated on your site. 
 In your WordPress dashboard, go to Plugins → Add New and search for Free Widgets For Elementor . 
 Click Install Now , then Activate . 
 Open any page in the Elementor editor. A new Free Widgets category appears at the top of the widgets panel. 
 Drag any widget onto your page and start customising it. 

 Search for Free Widgets For Elementor under Plugins → Add New. 

 After activating, a Free Widgets category appears at the top of the Elementor widgets panel. 

## What is inside

 Eight widgets, each filling one gap in the free Elementor core: 

 Widget What it is for 

 Pricing Table Header, price, feature list, button, and an optional "featured" highlight 
 Flip Box A 3D hover or click flip to a back face with a call to action 
 Team Photo, role, bio and social links for team member cards 
 Call To Action Title, text, button and background in a styled box 
 Countdown Timer Counts down to a date and time, with an optional expired message 
 Post Grid A responsive grid of posts — image, title, meta, excerpt, read-more 
 Logo Carousel A responsive logo or brand carousel with arrows, dots and autoplay 
 Table of Contents An auto-generated, clickable page outline with smooth scroll and scrollspy 

 Every setting sits in the normal Elementor sidebar, so there is nothing new to learn, and all the widgets are built to work inside Elementor's flexbox and grid containers. 

 The Pricing Table widget, with one plan marked as featured. 

 The Flip Box and Team widgets side by side. 

## Using the demo library

 Instead of building sections from scratch, the plugin includes an optional Demo Library — a one-click way to import ready-made Elementor sections, images included, built with these widgets. New demos are added over time without needing a plugin update. 
 To use it, open the plugin's Demo Library screen from the WordPress admin, browse the available sections, and click Import on the one you want. If you are curious how that works under the hood, I wrote about it in [the demo library case study](/blog/shared-demo-library-for-wordpress-plugins/). 

 Ready-made sections you can import in one click, images included. 

## Why it stays fast

 Eight widgets could easily mean eight widgets' worth of CSS and JavaScript on every page. It does not, for one reason: each widget's files load only on pages where that widget is actually used. A page with just a countdown timer never downloads the pricing table styles, the carousel engine, or anything else it does not render. 
 There is no jQuery dependency and no shared heavy library underneath — plain CSS and vanilla JavaScript per widget. That is the whole performance story: not clever optimisation, just never shipping what the page does not need. 

## Widget mistakes that cost you speed

 Installing without Elementor active. This plugin extends Elementor, so the free Elementor plugin has to be installed and active first. 
 Expecting a Pro upsell. There is not one. If a widget looks locked, that is not this plugin — double check which plugin you installed. 
 Assuming it needs Elementor Pro. It does not. Everything works on the free version. 

## FAQ

 Does this plugin require Elementor Pro? 
 No. It only requires the free version of Elementor. 

 Will it slow down my site? 
 No. Each widget's CSS and JavaScript load only on the specific pages where that widget is used. 

 Is it really free forever? 
 Yes. No Pro version, no licence key, no locked features. 

 Does it work with Elementor's flexbox and grid containers? 
 Yes, all the widgets are built to work inside Elementor containers. 

 I activated the plugin but I do not see the "Free Widgets" category. What is wrong? 
 This almost always means the free Elementor plugin is not active yet. Activate Elementor first, then reload the page editor — the category will appear at the top of the widgets panel. 

## Conclusion

 If you have ever reached for a bloated all-in-one addon pack just to get one pricing table or countdown widget, Free Widgets For Elementor is meant to be the lighter alternative — the widgets Elementor's free core is missing, and nothing else. 
 
 [Download on WordPress.org](https://wordpress.org/plugins/free-widgets-for-elementor/)
 [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/devmonowar/free-widgets-for-elementor)

 General Slider guide 

# How to build a fast, accessible slider in WordPress with General Slider

 By Monowar Hossain 
 11 August 2026 

 Summary. Most WordPress slider plugins either load jQuery and a pile of unused CSS and JavaScript on every page, or lock the good design presets behind a Pro upgrade. General Slider is built on the lightweight Splide engine — no jQuery, accessible by default, and assets load only on pages that actually show a slider. 

## On this page

 [Why most sliders slow down every page](#problem) 
 [A slider that loads only where it is used](#solution) 
 [What you need to install it](#requirements) 
 [Installing General Slider](#install) 
 [Building your first slider](#first-slider) 
 [Design presets and skins](#design) 
 [What accessibility actually means here](#accessibility) 
 [Mistakes that break a new slider](#mistakes) 
 [FAQ](#faq) 
 [Conclusion](#conclusion) 

## Why most sliders slow down every page

 A slider sounds like a simple feature, but it is one of the most common places a WordPress site picks up weight it does not need — jQuery dependencies, render-blocking CSS, and JavaScript that runs on every page even when there is no slider on it. 
 Slower pages mean worse Core Web Vitals, and worse Core Web Vitals eventually means worse rankings. The frustrating part is that most of that cost is paid on pages that do not contain a slider at all. 

## A slider that loads only where it is used

 General Slider lets you build a reusable slider once, then drop it anywhere with a block, a shortcode, or an Elementor widget — no page builder and no code required. 
 It is built on [Splide](https://splidejs.com/), a lightweight slider engine with no dependencies, so there is no jQuery on the front end. Assets are added only to pages that actually contain a slider. 

## What you need to install it

 WordPress 6.0 or later 
 PHP 7.4 or later 
 No page builder required. The block and the shortcode work with any theme, and an Elementor widget is included automatically if Elementor is active. 

## Installing General Slider

 In your WordPress dashboard, go to Plugins → Add New and search for General Slider . 
 Click Install Now , then Activate . 
 Go to General Slider → Add New to build your first slider, or open General Slider → Settings to import a ready-made demo instead. 
 A starter demo is created automatically on first activation, so a fresh install already has something to look at. 

 Search for General Slider under Plugins → Add New, then install and activate it. 

 The edit screen: slide fields on the left, design preset and navigation skin on the right. 

## Building your first slider

 You can add slides by hand, or switch Slides source to Pull slides from posts (dynamic) and let the slider build itself from your latest posts, pages, or WooCommerce products. 
 Once the slider is published, embed it in any of three ways: 
 
 Block — add the General Slider block and pick your slider from the list. 
 Shortcode — [general_slider id="123"] 
 Elementor — drag in the General Slider widget. 
 
 The exact shortcode for each slider is shown on its own edit screen, so you never have to guess the ID. 

 A published hero slider on the front end, with arrows, dots and a pause control. 

## Design presets and skins

 Five design presets control the slide layout — hero, split, minimal, testimonial, fullscreen. Navigation and frame skins control the arrows, dots and frame, and you can mix any skin with any preset. 
 On top of that, each slide can have a background video, text entrance animations, and its own accent colour, all set from the slider's settings box. None of it needs code. 
 You can see every preset and skin side by side in the [demo library](https://devmonowar.github.io/wp-plugin-demo-library/general-slider/) before you build anything. 

 The demo library — six ready-made sliders, each a different preset and skin combination you can import in one click. 

## What accessibility actually means here

 The title of this guide promises an accessible slider, so here is exactly what that covers — four concrete behaviours, not a badge: 
 
 Keyboard navigation. Every control — arrows, dots, pause button — is reachable and operable by keyboard alone, in a logical order. If a visitor cannot use a mouse, the slider still fully works. 
 Screen-reader labels. Slides, controls and state changes are announced with proper labels, so the slider makes sense when heard instead of seen. Decorative elements are hidden from assistive technology rather than read out as noise. 
 A play and pause control for autoplay. A slider that moves on its own must be stoppable. Anyone who needs more time to read — or who finds motion distracting — gets a visible, obvious pause button. 
 Reduced-motion support. When the visitor's system asks for reduced motion, entrance animations and autoplay behaviour step back instead of playing anyway. The content stays fully available; only the movement is toned down. 
 
 None of this requires configuration. It ships in the plugin because most sliders treat accessibility as a premium feature, and I think a slider that locks out some visitors is simply unfinished. 

## Mistakes that break a new slider

 Forgetting to publish the slider. A slider has to be published, not saved as a draft, before it will appear on the front end. This is the single most common support question I get. 
 Pointing the block or shortcode at the wrong slider. Check that the ID matches the slider you meant. The correct shortcode is printed on each slider's edit screen. 
 Not clearing the cache. If you use a caching plugin and your changes do not show up, clear the site cache after editing a slider. 

## FAQ

 Does it load jQuery? 
 No. The front end uses the lightweight, dependency-free Splide engine. 

 Will it slow down my site? 
 No. CSS and JavaScript load only on pages that contain a slider, images are lazy-loaded, and a slider only initialises once it is scrolled into view. 

 Do I need Elementor? 
 No. A dedicated Elementor widget is included if Elementor is active, but the block and the shortcode work with any theme. 

 Can I build a slider automatically from my posts? 
 Yes. Switch Slides source to dynamic and pick posts, pages, or WooCommerce products. 

## Conclusion

 If your current slider plugin is adding weight to pages that do not even use it, that is exactly the problem General Slider was built to fix — a fast, accessible slider that only loads where it is actually needed. 
 
 [Download on WordPress.org](https://wordpress.org/plugins/general-slider/)
 [Source on GitHub](https://github.com/devmonowar/general-slider)
 [Browse the demos](https://devmonowar.github.io/wp-plugin-demo-library/general-slider/)
